q: what is the difference between a nebula and a galaxy
how are nebula and galaxy different
a: A nebula and a galaxy are two very different astronomical objects, often confused because both appear as fuzzy patches of light in the night sky. A nebula (plural: nebulae) is a cloud of gas and dust in space, often spanning tens to hundreds of light-years across. Nebulae are star-forming regions where gravity pulls gas and dust together to form new stars. Examples include the Orion Nebula, the Eagle Nebula, and the Crab Nebula. There are different types: emission nebulae (glow from ionized gas), reflection nebulae (reflect starlight), dark nebulae (absorb light), and planetary nebulae (expelled from dying stars). A galaxy is a vast, gravitationally bound system containing billions to trillions of stars, along with gas, dust, and dark matter. Galaxies are enormous, spanning thousands to hundreds of thousands of light-years across. Our Milky Way galaxy contains an estimated 100-400 billion stars and is about 100,000 light-years in diameter. Galaxies come in different shapes: spiral (like the Milky Way and Andromeda), elliptical, and irregular. The key difference is scale: a galaxy contains billions of stars, while a nebula is a relatively small cloud within a galaxy where stars form or die. You could fit millions of nebulae inside a single galaxy. Nebulae are visible within our own galaxy, while other galaxies are separate island universes far beyond the Milky Way.
